claim: The CORE-Bench authors describe their correctness rule for reproduction tasks.
quote: We determine if an agent correctly solves a task if the agent's reported results for all questions fall within a 95% prediction interval for every task question of the results from the three manual runs (although only 17 / 181 task questions have stochastic answers).

claim: The CORE-Bench authors say that building the benchmark on public repositories permits periodic updates.
quote: CORE-Bench's foundation in public repositories enables periodic updates of the benchmark tasks, which could mitigate concerns about contamination and saturation.

claim: A later case study of CORE-Bench reports that the benchmark had construct-validity problems.
quote: First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents.

claim: PaperBench grades replications against hierarchical rubrics with an LLM judge.
quote: To enable scalable evaluation, we also develop an LLM-based judge to automatically grade replication attempts against rubrics, and assess our judge's performance by creating a separate benchmark for judges.

claim: The PaperBench authors report how well their best judge matches human graders.
quote: Our best LLM-based judge, which uses o3-mini-high with custom scaffolding, achieves an F1 score of 0.83 on the auxiliary evaluation, suggesting that this judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human judge.

claim: The PaperBench authors also acknowledge that judge accuracy needs further work.
quote: We've taken an early step with JudgeEval (Section 4.2) to measure the accuracy of model-based judges on tasks with huge complex outputs, but more work is needed to improve accuracy and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
locator: sec. A.2. Improving automated judges, para 104

claim: SciReplicate-Bench addresses contamination by its choice of paper dates.
quote: This recent publication window was deliberately chosen to minimize the risk of data leakage.

claim: A study of repeated identical evaluations found that pairwise preferences flip often.
quote: Across judges, pairwise preferences flip on average 13.6% of the time, with 28% of questions exceeding a 20% flip rate and one question reaching 56%.

claim: Work on clinical agents argues that benchmarks typically score one run per task.
quote: Such agents order tests, request medications and place referrals, yet benchmarks typically score one run per task and rarely ask whether identical inputs produce identical actions

claim: FIRE-Bench reports high variance across runs for research agents.
quote: even the strongest agents achieve limited rediscovery success (<50 F1), exhibit high variance across runs, and display recurring failure modes in experimental design, execution, and evidence-based reasoning.

claim: RQ-Bench found that LLM judges consistently rate model-generated research questions as highly novel, which the authors call a novelty mirage.
quote: LLM judges consistently rate model-generated RQs as highly novel, producing a novelty mirage

claim: A study of novelty judges reports that prompt wording can strongly change verdicts.
quote: simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not must change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown

claim: HindSight reports that its future-impact scores correlate negatively with LLM-judged novelty.
quote: Moreover, HindSight scores are \emph{negatively} correlated with LLM-judged novelty ($ρ{=}{-}0.29$, $p{<}0.01$), suggesting that LLMs systematically overvalue novel-sounding ideas that never materialize in real research.

claim: A large human study found LLM ideas were judged more novel than expert ideas.
quote: we find LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas while being judged slightly weaker on feasibility.

claim: OpenNovelty instead grounds novelty assessments in retrieved prior work.
quote: Unlike naive LLM-based approaches, \textsc{OpenNovelty} grounds all assessments in retrieved real papers, ensuring verifiable judgments.

claim: A survey of 80 AI-scientist systems states that LLM judging is the dominant evaluator.
quote: Second, LLM-as-judge is the most common evaluator across the corpus, so most outputs remain candidates rather than findings

claim: A contamination survey cautions that an LLM used for evaluation may itself be contaminated.
quote: Automatic evaluation can mitigate some effects of BDC by employing self-supervised methods that reduce reliance on labeled data, but this approach cannot completely eliminate the risk of contamination, for example, the LLM used for automatic evaluation may also suffers from the BDC problem.
